name: Lunds Konsthall
overview: Municipal art hall at Mårtenstorget 3 in Lund, about a 10-minute walk from Lund Central Station; the site's footer calls it "en del av Lunds kommun" (a part of Lund municipality; translation ours) (Lunds konsthall website).
Opened on 21 September 1957 with the exhibition "Svensk nutidskonst"; it mainly shows Swedish and Nordic contemporary art, with one or more international shows a year (Swedish Wikipedia).

Building: designed by the Lund architect Klas Anshelm, with alternating high and low rooms, separate spaces for sculpture and large pictures, and open balconies (Swedish Wikipedia). The English history page gives about 650 square metres on two floors around an open atrium and some 50,000 visitors a year (Lunds konsthall website).
funding_verdict: Lunds Konsthall: municipal: Lund municipality
wider_context: On 10 December 2015 Lund's culture and leisure board decided to close the hall with the aim of reopening it later in reconstructed form (Swedish Wikipedia). The board said the hall would be adapted to "the present and future Lund" (Kunstkritikk).
Board chairman Joakim Friberg (Social Democrat) said the reconstruction was unrelated to the savings and followed a Cultural Council decision of 26 November 2015 (Kunstkritikk).
The protest was aimed at the hall's own owner, Lund municipality; the hall stayed open, and Nacking now heads Lunds konst, which runs its exhibitions.

press_items.title: Frida Sandström, "The End of Lund's Konsthall as We Know It" (2015)
"An open letter in support of Lunds konsthall" (2015)
Anders Kreuger, "Lund's Konsthall: Time and Again" (2016)

name: Malmö Konsthall
overview: Municipal contemporary art hall at S:t Johannesgatan 7, by Triangeln station, about a 15-minute walk from Malmö Central; it is part of the City of Malmö's culture administration (Kulturförvaltningen) (Malmö Konsthall website).

Opened on 22 March 1975 with a Munch exhibition and the group show "Ögon-Blickar/New Media 1". In 1931 members of Skånes Konstförening set up a foundation and a lottery to build a hall, a plan never carried out; the city decided in 1971 to build a municipal one (Malmö Konsthall, history page).

Building: Klas Anshelm won the competition; the hall has a large north-facing skylight and over 500 roof lanterns whose light can be shut off one by one (Malmö Konsthall, architecture page). Wikipedia says it was built from 1971 to 1974 in concrete, glass, wood and aluminium and won the 1974 Kasper Salin Prize.
funding_verdict: Malmö Konsthall: public: a unit of the City of Malmö's culture administration

name: Bonniers Konsthall
overview: Contemporary art gallery at Torsgatan 19, Stockholm, opened in 2006. It describes itself as having given space to contemporary art "förutsättningslöst", without conditions, since the doors opened (Bonniers Konsthall press release, 2022; translation).

The konsthall has its roots in the Maria Bonnier Dahlin Foundation, which Jeanette Bonnier (died 2016) founded in 1985 in memory of her daughter. The first exhibition in September 2006 showed all earlier grant recipients (Bonniers Konsthall website). The foundation awards grants to young artists every year (e-flux).
It is run by the Bonnier family as part of the Bonnier Group, "one of Scandinavia's biggest media groups" (Bonniers Konsthall website).
funding_verdict: Bonniers Konsthall: family-funded: a foundation from Jeanette Bonnier's estate, with the konsthall run by the Bonnier family within the Bonnier Group media business

name: Bildmuseet
overview: Contemporary art museum of Umeå University on the Umeälven riverbank, in the university's arts campus (Konstnärligt campus), a five-minute walk from central Umeå (museum website). It shows Swedish and international contemporary art, visual culture, design and architecture (Wikipedia).
Founded in 1981 by Umeå University, which still owns it (Wikipedia). After 30 years of operation it moved to a new building in 2012. The new building opened to the public on 19 May 2012.

Building: seven storeys, designed by Henning Larsen Architects with White Architects, clad in larch that is expected to fade to grey (Wikipedia). The arts campus was a collaboration between Umeå University and the developer Balticgruppen Design AB (Umeå University news, December 2010).
funding_verdict: Bildmuseet: mainly public: Umeå University (a state university), with municipal, regional and foundation grants

name: HEK (Haus der Elektronischen Künste)
overview: Museum for digital and media art at Freilager-Platz 9, Münchenstein / Basel. Tram 11 from Bahnhof SBB stops at "Freilager" (museums.ch).
Founded in 2011 on the Dreispitz site, a former warehouse area redeveloped by the Christoph Merian Foundation. Sabine Himmelsbach has directed it since 2012 (Wikipedia).
In 2014 it moved to Freilager-Platz and reopened on 21 November after more than a year of construction (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: HEK: public funding from the two Basel cantons (and the Swiss federal culture office until its 2018 cut), plus an award foundation and a corporate award partner

name: Musée d'Art et d'Histoire (MAH)
aliases: Musée d'art et d'histoire de Genève
Museum of Art and History Geneva
overview: The City of Geneva's encyclopedic museum at Rue Charles-Galland 2, with about 650,000 objects covering 15,000 years (stated by the space).
Founded in 1910, with the Musée Rath, the Maison Tavel and the Bibliothèque d'art et d'archéologie attached to it.
Its collection joins archaeology, fine arts, graphic arts, applied arts, watchmaking, jewellery and coins.
funding_verdict: Musée d'art et d'histoire: mainly public: the City of Geneva, with foundations, banks and watchmakers thanked for project support

name: Fotomuseum Winterthur
overview: Photography museum at Grüzenstrasse 44 and 45, Winterthur, run as the Stiftung Fotomuseum Winterthur (the museum's partners page; Wikipedia).
Founded in 1993 by the photographer George Reinhart, a nephew of the art collector Oskar Reinhart (Wikipedia).

Since autumn 2003 it has run the Center of Photography with Fotostiftung Schweiz, sharing a bistro, library, seminar rooms and shop. The Center occupies two buildings on opposite sides of Grüzenstrasse, with about 1,000 m2 of exhibition area (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Fotomuseum Winterthur: mainly private and self-earned, with about one third public money from the Canton of Zurich and the City of Winterthur

name: Juming Museum
overview: Sculpture park and museum at No. 2 Xishi Lake, Jinshan District, New Taipei City. The museum says the site covers 11 hectares, of which 8 are open to visitors.

Founded by the sculptor Ju Ming (born 1938, died 2023), who began turning barren land in Jinshan into a park and museum in 1987. It opened on 19 September 1999 after twelve years of work (museum's founder page, Wikipedia).
Named for its founder. The operator is the Ju Ming Culture and Education Foundation (財團法人朱銘文教基金會).
funding_verdict: Juming Museum: founder-funded, now run by a foundation on admissions, donations and exhibition sponsors

name: National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts
overview: State art museum at No. 2, Section 1, Wuquan West Road, West District, Taichung, known as NTMoFA; Chinese name Guoli Taiwan Meishuguan (國立臺灣美術館; romanisation ours) (museum website; English Wikipedia).

Opened on 26 June 1988 under the Taiwan Provincial Government's education department as the Museum of Art; it closed in 1999 after damage in the 921 earthquake and reopened in July 2004 (English Wikipedia).
It came under the Council of Cultural Affairs, restructured as the Ministry of Culture on 20 May 2012 (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts: mainly public: Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, with small outside gifts
wider_context: August 2026 naming dispute at the 16th Gwangju Biennale: the pavilion's curator Chen Xiang-Wen and nine artists said on 15 August that the proposal the museum submitted as "Taiwan Pavilion" had been renamed "NTMoFA" without their consent (The Art Newspaper, 26 August 2026).

The Gwangju Biennale Foundation said the museum signed on 12 January 2026 as an institutional participant, so the pavilion bore its name; Taiwan's Ministry of Culture said the name had been agreed in an agreement signed on 2 April and called the foundation's account wrong (Central News Agency, 19 August 2026; The Art Newspaper).

The artists, the ministry and twenty other contributors called the change "political censorship"; the organisers said they considered the listing an administrative convention (ArtReview, 2026). On 25 August the foundation approved the "Taiwan Pavilion" name (The Art Newspaper).
Gwangju art groups backed the Taiwanese side and covered "NTMoFA" with "Taiwan" on a poster (udn, Central News Agency, 24 August 2026).
Connection: the objection was aimed at the biennale foundation; the museum was the pavilion's organiser, and its acronym replaced Taiwan's name.

name: Hong-gah Museum
overview: Private contemporary art museum (鳳甲美術館) on the 11th floor of the Huan-Yu Trade Building, 166 Daye Road, Beitou District, Taipei. It is within walking distance west of Qiyan Station on the Taipei Metro Red Line (hong-gah.org.tw, Wikipedia).
Founded by the businessman and collector Chiu Tsai-hsing (Andrew Chew). It opened to the public on 25 October 1999 and moved to its current floor in 2008 (hong-gah.org.tw, Wikipedia).
Named for Chiu's father, Chiu Feng-chia (邱鳳甲) (Chew's Culture Foundation page).
funding_verdict: Hong-gah Museum: self-funded: founder Chiu Tsai-hsing's private money

name: MOCA Taipei
overview: Contemporary art museum at No. 39 Chang-An West Road, Datong District, Taipei, within walking distance southwest of Zhongshan Station on the Taipei Metro (MOCA Taipei, Wikipedia).
Opened in May 2001 and described as the first art institution in Taiwan dedicated exclusively to contemporary art (Ministry of Education art education site, Wikipedia).

The building was completed in 1921, in the Japanese colonial period, as Kensei Elementary School. After 1945 it housed Taipei City Government offices. It was designated a municipal historic site in 1996, and the rest of the building is occupied by Jian Cheng Junior High School (Ministry of Education site, Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: MOCA Taipei: public-owned, privately operated: run by the Taipei Culture Foundation since 2008, with corporate sponsors

press_items.title: no author named, "MoCA Taipei Embroiled in Dispute over Nearly Canceled Show" (16 August 2021)
no author named, "Row between artist Jun Yang and MoCA Taipei stirs controversy in Taiwan's artworld" (17 August 2021)
Michael Turton, "Notes from Central Taiwan: No place for official insularity" (23 August 2021)

name: Palais de Lomé
overview: Contemporary art and culture centre in a restored colonial-era palace in Lomé, standing in a botanical park of 11 hectares (The Art Newspaper) or ten hectares (French Wikipedia), with more than 40 bird species (The Art Newspaper).
Opened to the public on 28 November 2019 as Togo's first major contemporary art and culture centre (The Art Newspaper, Julia Michalska, 2019). The director is Sonia Lawson.

Earlier names and uses: Germany built the palace between 1898 and 1905 as the governor's residence. French governors later used it. After independence in 1960 it housed the presidency until 1970, briefly served as the prime minister's residence in September 1991, and was left abandoned for several years after damage in the political troubles, including an army attack in December 1991 (French Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Palais de Lomé: mainly public: the Togolese state, with corporate sponsors for events
wider_context: Ghanaian Times (citing the BBC, 1 July 2025): civil rights groups say at least seven people were killed in a crackdown on protesters who want Gnassingbé to step down; protests have been banned since 2022; the government called them a "campaign of disinformation and hatred" orchestrated from abroad.

TimesLIVE (citing Reuters, 1 July 2025): twelve civil society groups accused security forces of "shocking violence"; the government attributed the bodies recovered from a lagoon and a lake to drowning; authorities arrested dozens of people on 5 and 6 June, which Amnesty International described as a crackdown on dissent.
Gnassingbé became President of the Council of Ministers in May 2025, a post with no fixed term limit (TimesLIVE).
The centre was built with state money and opened with Gnassingbé present.

press_items.title: Claude Grunitzky, "Why this new museum is putting Togo on the map" (2019)
Julia Michalska, "Togo opens arts centre in former colonial palace" (2019)

name: Alice Yard
overview: Artist-run contemporary art space and network in Port of Spain. Since 2020 it has been based at Granderson Lab, 24 Erthig Road, Belmont (stated by the space).

Began in September 2006 during "Galvanise", a six-week art and performance programme (Caribbean Beat). The space's own site says people were first welcomed on 15 September 2006. A non-profit incorporated under the law of Trinidad and Tobago (stated by the space).
The yard was the backyard of Alice, the great-grandmother of the architect Sean Leonard (Caribbean Beat).
funding_verdict: Alice Yard: mixed small funding: a US foundation grant plus project support from Nordic and local bodies and two named local firms
wider_context: Wikipedia's documenta fifteen page describes an antisemitism controversy: in January 2022 the blog Alliance Against Anti-Semitism Kassel made claims of ties to the BDS movement against documenta; a forum planned for May was cancelled on 4 May; the show opened on 18 June 2022; a mural was covered and taken down after the opening; and general director Sabine Schormann resigned on 17 July 2022.

The Wikipedia page names Alice Yard once, in its list of participants, with no further context, and does not name it in the controversy. Artviewer (3 September 2022) says Alice Yard hosted a residency programme for the 100 days of the show.

name: Le 32Bis
overview: Cultural association and art centre at 32 bis, rue Ben Ghedhahem, in the centre of Tunis, dedicated to research, creation, exhibition and the sharing of knowledge (32bis.org).

Opened as a new contemporary art centre in February 2022 with the exhibition "WIRD" by the Franco-Algerian artist Bruno Hadjih, which ran from 18 February to 18 March 2022. Camille Lévy was artistic director at that time (Managers, 17 February 2022). In 2026 La Presse describes Hela Djebbi as curator and director.

La Presse says the building was converted into an art centre by an association from 2016 (La Presse, Amel Bouslama, 2 January 2026). A gallery called Le 32 BIS opened on 5 June 2015 on rue Ali Ben Ghedahem in a three-storey former Philips building (Kapitalis). Kapitalis calls Yosr Ben Ammar and Mehdi Ben Cheikh the two gallery directors (Kapitalis, Fawz Ben Ali, 9 June 2015).
funding_verdict: Le 32Bis: private patronage: an association funded by private patrons, according to its artistic director

name: Musée National du Bardo
overview: Archaeology and history museum in Le Bardo, Tunis, in a 19th-century Ottoman governor's palace near the parliament (AFP via Al-Monitor, 14 September 2023). Wikipedia dates the palace to the 15th-century Hafsid period, later a beylical palace.
Proposed in the 1860s by Muhammad Khaznadar and opened on 7 May 1888 as the Alaoui Museum, after the reigning bey. It took the Bardo name after independence (Wikipedia).
Collections: Roman mosaics, marble statues, Libyco-Punic artefacts, Greek works from the Mahdia shipwreck and Islamic pieces such as the Blue Qur'an of Kairouan (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Musée National du Bardo: state museum: a World Bank loan behind the 2009 to 2012 expansion and corporate patrons of the Louvre partnership

press_items.title: Houcine Jaïdi, "Musée du Bardo (2012-2022) : la décennie de tous les malheurs" (16 May 2022)

name: Pera Museum
overview: Private art museum in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul, near İstiklal Avenue and Taksim Square (Wikipedia).
Founded by the Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation and established on 8 June 2005 (Wikipedia).
Housed in the former Bristol Hotel, built in 1893 to designs by Achille Manoussos. Architect Sinan Genim renovated it from 2003 to 2005 and kept the facade (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Pera Museum (Istanbul): private: founded by a family foundation, the Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation

name: 421 Arts Campus (formerly Warehouse421)
overview: Arts campus in the Mina Zayed port district of Abu Dhabi, at Zayed Port next to the Abu Dhabi Vegetable Market and Mina Center. It describes itself as an independent platform for emerging artists and creative practitioners in the UAE and the region.

Established in 2015 as Warehouse421 in a renovated warehouse. Since renamed 421. Backed by the Salama bint Hamdan Al Nahyan Foundation (The Gazelle, 2017; Gulf News, 2018). Faisal Al Hassan is general manager (The National, 2021).
Earlier name: Warehouse421. The building sits between warehouses 422 and 423 and has no number plate of its own (The Gazelle).
funding_verdict: 421 Arts Campus: privately funded by a royal family foundation

name: Ishara Art Foundation
overview: Non-profit art foundation for South Asian contemporary art at 3 Alserkal Avenue, Street 17, Al Quoz 1, Dubai, in a two-storey warehouse space (Ishara; The National, 2019).

Founded by Smita Prabhakar, its chairperson (Ishara). It opened on 18 March 2019 (The National, 18 March 2019). ArtAsiaPacific (18 January 2019) called it the first non-profit institution in the UAE dedicated to art and artists from South Asia.
The space is modular and adapts to each show. Prabhakar said "We spent a fortune on lighting" (The National, 2024).
funding_verdict: Ishara Art Foundation: self-funded: founder Smita Prabhakar, from her business interests
wider_context: Trustee Abdulfattah Sharaf: the Ishara board page lists him as "Chairman, HSBC Bank Middle East Limited". Gulf News (page last updated 27 April 2023) reported his appointment as chairman of HSBC Bank Middle East from 1 May.

On 11 December 2012 HSBC reached a deferred-prosecution agreement with the US Department of Justice in a money-laundering case and agreed to pay $1.92 billion, with an independent monitor under a five-year agreement (Fox Business). His seat is a board seat; no reporting found that HSBC funds Ishara.

Trustee Mustafa Al Hashimi: the Ishara board page lists him as "Chief Executive Officer, Wasl Hospitality and Leisure". Wikipedia describes Wasl as a semi-government company established on 25 May 2008 by the Dubai Real Estate Corporation and lists Wasl Hospitality & Leisure among its subsidiaries.

name: Tashkeel
overview: Studio, gallery and residency organisation for visual artists and designers in the UAE, with its main site in Nad Al Sheba, Dubai, and a makerspace at Unit 89, Alserkal Avenue, Al Quoz (stated by the space).
Founded in 2008 by Sheikha Lateefa bint Maktoum bin Rashid Al Maktoum (stated by the space).

Wikipedia describes the main site as a 2,800 square metre building constructed in 1987, with a gallery, studios for fine art, digital work, 3D, photography, printmaking and textile printing, a darkroom, a library, a lounge and a garden. Wikipedia also lists a traditional house in Al Fahidi with five artist studios and two gallery spaces.
funding_verdict: Tashkeel: founded by Sheikha Lateefa bint Maktoum bin Rashid Al Maktoum, with income from its own consulting and retail services and project partners

name: Hospitalfield
overview: Arts centre, historic house and garden in Arbroath, Angus, run by the Hospitalfield Trust, a registered Scottish charity (SC009987).
In the 13th century the monks of Arbroath Abbey built a hospital on the site to receive pilgrims (Hospitalfield history pages).

The painter Patrick Allan married Elizabeth Fraser, the last heir to the estate, in 1843. The couple left their estates and collections in trust to support artists and education in the arts, and when Allan-Fraser died in 1890 the trustees took over management of Hospitalfield (Hospitalfield history pages).
funding_verdict: Hospitalfield: grant-funded: public and lottery bodies, with charitable trusts: Creative Scotland, National Lottery Heritage Fund, Historic Environment Scotland and the Scottish Government's Tay Cities Deal
